reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard haematology references
clinicalPearls: A selective failure of erythropoiesis characterised by severe anaemia, reticulocytopenia, and near-absent erythroid precursors in an otherwise normal bone marrow
White cells and platelets are typically preserved, which distinguishes it from aplastic anaemia and most marrow infiltrative disorders

Acquired PRCA is often immune-mediated and may be idiopathic or secondary to thymoma, lymphoproliferative disorders (notably large granular lymphocyte leukaemia and CLL), autoimmune disease, drugs, or pregnancy

Parvovirus B19 causes PRCA by directly infecting erythroid progenitors, producing transient aplasia in the healthy but persistent aplasia in the immunocompromised and aplastic crises in chronic haemolysis
Erythropoietin therapy has rarely triggered antibody-mediated PRCA through neutralising anti-erythropoietin antibodies
Evaluation should include imaging for thymoma and screening for an underlying lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disorder
Management principles are treating the underlying cause (for example thymectomy or antiviral immunoglobulin for parvovirus), transfusion support, and immunosuppression for immune-mediated disease
Bone marrow examination confirming isolated erythroid hypoplasia is central to diagnosis
It is distinct from the inherited Diamond-Blackfan anaemia, which presents in infancy
reference.pathophysiology: Pure red cell aplasia is a selective arrest of erythroid production with sparing of other haematopoietic lineages. In acquired immune-mediated disease, autoreactive T cells or antibodies target erythroid progenitors or erythropoietin, halting red cell production; this may be idiopathic or driven by an associated thymoma, clonal lymphoproliferative disorder (such as large granular lymphocyte leukaemia), autoimmune condition, drug or pregnancy. Parvovirus B19 causes PRCA by directly infecting and lysing erythroid progenitor cells via the P antigen receptor. The result in all cases is profound anaemia with reticulocytopenia while granulocytes and platelets remain normal.
additionalDifferentials: Aplastic anaemia (pancytopenia rather than isolated anaemia)
Anaemia of chronic disease or renal failure
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and reticulocyte count confirming isolated anaemia with reticulocytopenia
Bone marrow examination showing selective erythroid hypoplasia
CT of the chest to detect thymoma; investigations for lymphoproliferative disease including T-cell clonality studies
Autoimmune and drug history review; anti-erythropoietin antibody testing when relevant
redFlags: Severe symptomatic anaemia requiring urgent transfusion
Underlying thymoma or lymphoproliferative malignancy identified on workup
Persistent parvovirus B19 aplasia in an immunocompromised patient
Aplastic crisis in a patient with chronic haemolytic anaemia
Complications of transfusional iron overload with chronic dependence
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause: parvovirus-associated aplasia in immunocompetent patients is self-limiting, and immune-mediated PRCA often responds to immunosuppression or treatment of the associated disorder, though relapse is common. Cases linked to malignancy or refractory to therapy may cause chronic transfusion dependence with attendant iron overload.
pitfalls: Missing an underlying thymoma or lymphoproliferative disorder
Overlooking parvovirus B19 as a treatable cause, especially in the immunocompromised or those with haemolysis
Confusing PRCA with aplastic anaemia by not noting preserved white cell and platelet counts
Failing to review drugs, including erythropoietin, as potential triggers
Neglecting iron overload monitoring in transfusion-dependent patients
